title: Controlled drugs and safe storage
blurb: Place common drugs in the right Misuse of Drugs Regulations schedule, keep the CD register correctly, and store, check and dispose of medicines safely.
question: A colleague asks you to countersign the controlled drugs register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine she has already prepared and given alone. What should you do?

teach.body: Controlled drugs (CDs) are medicines with potential for misuse or diversion, regulated by the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. The Regulations place each drug in one of five schedules, and the schedule decides how it is prescribed, recorded, stored and destroyed. In plain terms: the higher the risk of misuse (and lower the schedule number), the tighter the paperwork.
teach.cite: Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001; NICE NG46 (2016)

teach.caption: Morphine is Schedule 2, but preparations containing no more than 0.2% morphine (such as 10 mg in 5 mL oral solution) fall in Schedule 5. Many organisations still record them locally.

items: Name of the person having the dose.
Date and time of the dose.
Name, formulation and strength of the CD.
Name and signature or initials of the person who gave it, and of any witness.
If part of an ampoule is discarded: the amount given, the amount disposed of, and signatures of the person disposing and the witness.

teach.caption: A witness signs for what they saw. Signing for a dose you did not witness falsifies the record.

teach.body: If a stock check does not match the register, recount, check recent entries, and report the discrepancy promptly to the nurse in charge and pharmacy per the SOP. Destruction of Schedule 2 stock must be witnessed by an authorised person (regulation 27), so out-of-date stock is kept segregated and recorded until then. Patients' own medicines, including CDs, are returned to a pharmacy for disposal, for example after a death at home.

teach.caption: Green Book ch3: read the maximum, minimum and current temperatures daily, record and sign, reset the thermometer, and react and document if outside +2°C to +8°C.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurses Kemi and Sam
teach.body: Sam asks Kemi to countersign the register for subcutaneous morphine she prepared and gave alone 10 minutes ago. Kemi did not see the dose checked, drawn up or given, so she declines and offers to witness the next dose from preparation onwards. She advises Sam to tell the nurse in charge so the record can be completed honestly under policy. Later, at the weekly stock check, both nurses count and sign the balance.

teach.text: The register keeps for 2 YEARS from the LAST entry (not from the first, and not 7 years). And remember: midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3, not 2, while oxycodone and fentanyl are Schedule 2.

items: Schedule 2: morphine, diamorphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone. Schedule 3: midazolam, temazepam, tramadol, gabapentin, pregabalin, buprenorphine.
Separate register per premises storing Schedule 2 CDs; keep 2 years from the last entry.
Stock checks per SOP, usually at least weekly, ideally 2 people; report discrepancies promptly.
Record patient, date and time, drug, form, strength, dose, signatures; witness discards.
Fridge +2°C to +8°C, read and record daily; act and document if outside the range.

summary: You can now place common controlled drugs in their schedules and keep a CD register to NICE NG46 standards. You can also handle witnessing, discrepancies, destruction and safe storage of medicines, including the fridge.

A.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Which of these is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
options: Midazolam 10 mg in 2 mL solution for injection
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Diazepam 5 mg tablets
A.why: Oxycodone is Schedule 2 under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, so it is recorded in the CD register.

A.q: A ward's CD register has been completed and a new book started. How long must the old register be kept?
options: 2 years from the date of the last entry
1 year from the first entry
5 years from the date of the first entry
7 years from the date of the last entry
A.why: NICE NG46: controlled drugs registers must be kept for 2 years from the date of the last entry.

whyNot.1: 1 year is too short, and the period runs from the last entry.
whyNot.2: 5 years is not the requirement, and it runs from the last entry.
whyNot.3: 7 years is suggested for records of destroying patients' own CDs, not the register.

A.q: At 07:30 the ward medicines fridge reads 11°C and the overnight maximum was 13°C. It holds insulin pens and influenza vaccines. What should the nurse do?
options: Reset the thermometer and continue to use the stock
Discard all of the fridge stock immediately into the nearest sharps bin
Move everything to the freezer to cool it quickly
Separate the stock, report it and seek pharmacy advice before use
A.why: Temperatures outside +2°C to +8°C require action and documentation. The stock must not be used until pharmacy or the manufacturer advises (Green Book ch3).

whyNot.0: Resetting without acting hides a cold chain breach; the stock may be ineffective.
whyNot.1: Stock may still be usable after advice; immediate disposal into sharps bins is wasteful and the wrong stream.

B.q: Nurse Kemi is asked to countersign the CD register for a dose of subcutaneous morphine that a colleague prepared and gave alone 10 minutes ago. What should Kemi do?
options: Sign it, as her colleague is experienced and trusted
Sign it, and add a note that she did not see it given
Decline, and offer to witness the next dose from preparation onwards
Sign it after first checking that the remaining ampoule count is correct
B.why: A witness signs for what they observed. Signing for an administration she did not witness would falsify the record (NG46 1.7.4; Code 10.3).

whyNot.0: Trust in a colleague does not make a retrospective witness signature honest.
whyNot.1: A witness signature with a disclaimer is still not a witnessed administration.
whyNot.3: A correct count does not show what dose was given or to whom.

B.q: During a weekly stock check, two nurses find the oxycodone 5 mg capsule count is one lower than the register balance. What should they do first?
options: Amend the balance to match the stock and sign it
Wait until next week's check to see if it is found
Borrow a capsule from another ward to correct the stock level
Recount, check recent entries, then report it per the SOP
B.why: Discrepancies are investigated and reported under the SOP (NG46 1.1.12-1.1.13). Recounting and checking recent entries comes first, then prompt reporting.

whyNot.0: Altering the balance conceals the discrepancy.
whyNot.1: Delaying a week risks losing evidence and further diversion.
whyNot.2: Borrowing stock hides the loss and creates a second discrepancy.

B.q: Eileen, 76, is prescribed morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously. The ward stocks morphine 10 mg in 1 mL ampoules. A second nurse witnesses throughout. What is recorded?
options: 2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; 7.5 mg (0.75 mL) discarded, both signatures
10 mg given, as the whole ampoule was opened
2.5 mg (0.25 mL) given; the discarded 7.5 mg does not need recording
2.5 mg (2.5 mL) given; the rest returned to the cupboard
B.why: 2.5 / 10 x 1 = 0.25 mL. NG46 asks for the amount given, the amount disposed of and the signatures of the person disposing and the witness.

whyNot.1: The record must show the dose actually given, not the ampoule size.
whyNot.2: Disposed amounts must be recorded with signatures.
whyNot.3: 2.5 mL is a tenfold volume error, and opened ampoules are not returned to stock.

C.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with a colleague as witness. What is correct?
options: Destroy them now in the denaturing kit with any registered nurse as witness
Flush them down the sink with two nurses present
Return them to stock until pharmacy collects them
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
C.why: Destruction of Schedule 2 stock CDs must be witnessed by an authorised person (MDR 2001 reg 27; NG46 1.8.3). Until then they are kept segregated and recorded.

whyNot.0: A ward colleague is not an authorised witness for Schedule 2 stock destruction.
whyNot.1: Flushing is not an approved method, and an authorised witness is still required.
whyNot.2: Expired stock should be segregated so it is not used in error.

C.q: After Arthur, 89, dies at home, his son asks the district nurse what to do with Arthur's remaining tablets, including modified-release morphine. What is the best advice?
options: Flush the tablets down the toilet
Return all the medicines to a community pharmacy for disposal
Keep them safely at home in case another relative needs them later
Put them in the household waste in a sealed bag
C.why: Patients' own medicines, including CDs, are returned to a community pharmacy for safe disposal; NG46 asks professionals to advise people how to dispose of CDs safely.

whyNot.0: Flushing is unsafe for the environment and not an approved route.
whyNot.2: Medicines belong to the person they were prescribed for; keeping them risks misuse.
whyNot.3: Household waste is not safe for CDs and risks diversion.

C.q: A nurse is about to give oral morphine to Mr Reid, who is alert. According to NICE NG46, what should she tell him before administration?
options: The name and dose of the drug
That it is his regular pain relief, without naming it
Its schedule under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations
The batch number on the bottle
C.why: NG46 1.7.2: tell the person the name and dose of the controlled drug before it is administered, unless circumstances prevent this.

whyNot.1: A vague description does not let him check the name and dose.
whyNot.2: The legal schedule is not the information NG46 asks you to share.
whyNot.3: The batch number is recorded where needed but is not the key information for the patient.

reteach.title: Count it, witness it, sign it
reteach.question: If an inspector checked one dose of morphine tomorrow, could the record prove exactly what happened?

blocks.h: The register is the CD's passport
blocks.body: Every Schedule 2 CD that enters, is given, is discarded or is destroyed must leave a trail: who, what, when, how much and who saw it. The register, stock checks and authorised witnesses exist so that any missing dose can be noticed quickly. A signature that is not true breaks the whole chain.

blocks.text: Schedule 2 = register and authorised witness for stock destruction. Schedule 3 midazolam and tramadol are controlled, but not Schedule 2.

explain.body: Sch 2: morphine, diamorphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone. Sch 3: midazolam, temazepam, tramadol, gabapentin, pregabalin, buprenorphine. Sch 4 Pt 1: diazepam, lorazepam, zopiclone.

test.q: In which schedule of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 is midazolam?
options: Schedule 2
Schedule 3
Schedule 4 Part 1
Schedule 5
test.why: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug (gov.uk controlled drugs list).

whyNot.0: Schedule 2 includes morphine and diamorphine, not midazolam.
whyNot.2: Schedule 4 Part 1 includes diazepam and lorazepam.
whyNot.3: Schedule 5 covers low-strength preparations such as some codeine products.

explain.body: One register per premises where Schedule 2 CDs are stored; entries for every dose with signatures; kept for 2 years from the last entry.

test.q: Which detail is required in the record of a controlled drug administration under NG46?
options: The patient's next of kin
The prescriber's professional registration number
The formulation and strength of the drug
The pharmacy's dispensing time
test.why: NG46 1.7.4 lists the name, formulation and strength of the CD alongside patient, date and time, dose and signatures.

whyNot.0: Next of kin is not part of the CD administration record.
whyNot.1: The prescriber's number is not listed in the administration record content.
whyNot.3: Dispensing time is not part of the administration record.

explain.body: Per SOP, usually at least weekly, ideally 2 people, balance against stock, dated and signed. Discrepancies are reported and investigated.

test.q: How often does NICE NG46 suggest most organisations carry out CD stock checks?
options: At least once a day
At least every 3 months
At least once a month
At least once a week
test.why: NG46 1.1.12: for most organisations stock checks should be at least once a week, adjusted by risk, ideally with 2 people.

whyNot.0: Daily checks may be chosen by risk assessment, but weekly is the stated norm.
whyNot.1: Quarterly checks are far too infrequent.
whyNot.2: Monthly is less often than NG46 suggests.

explain.body: CDs stored under the Safe Custody Regulations and local SOP. Fridge items at +2°C to +8°C with daily maximum, minimum and current readings recorded, thermometer reset, and action taken if outside range.

test.q: What temperature range should a medicines and vaccine fridge maintain?
options: 0°C to +4°C
+2°C to +8°C
test.why: The Green Book (ch3) specifies storage at +2°C to +8°C.

whyNot.0: Temperatures near 0°C risk freezing and damaging vaccines.
whyNot.2: Above +8°C is outside the safe range.
whyNot.3: This is room-temperature storage, not refrigeration.
